newsitem.title: FINLAND: UPM-Kymmene earnings fall in quarter.
newsitem.headline: UPM-Kymmene earnings fall in quarter.

text.p: Europe's largest forest products company, Finland's UPM-Kymmene Oy, said Thursday its profits edged lower in the latest quarter and voiced a more cautious view about the full year than some of its rivals.
Profit before special items and taxes fell 2 percent to 1.35 billion markka ($264 million) from 1.37 billion a year earlier. Sales fell to 13.1 billion markka ($2.6 billion) from 13.3 billion.
The company's caution reflected uncertainty in the pulp and paper markets, where sluggish demand and overcapacity have depressed prices, which just recently have started rising.
UPM said it expected 1997 earnings to be about the same as 1996, when pretax profits were 3.6 billion markka ($704 million).
That view contrasted with an expected improvement in full-year earnings from Finland's Metsa-Serla and a generally upbeat market view from Sweden's AssiDoman, which both reported earlier this week.

Asked about chances for higher earnings this year, Chief Executive Juha Niemela said: "There is a good possibility for that. But to be on the cautious side we see that we will reach about the same level as we did last year.
"Surprises to the negative side are also possible, but not as likely as they are to the opposite direction," he said in an interview.
UPM-Kymmene said strong economic growth in Europe would underpin an increase in paper consumption, but it voiced fears of overcapacity in fine paper in the second half.
"Sales prices for printing and writing papers are expected to rise, although only marginally during the first half of the year," the company said.
In fine paper, it said European production capacity threatened to rise faster than demand in the second half.
On newsprint, UPM-Kymmene said European prices were expected to benefit later this year from a rise in consumption and prices, already under way in North America.
While some analysts agreed, others saw more stability -- continuing the broad uncertainty which has been a hallmark of pulp and paper markets in recent months.
